extracted.intended_audience: general readers and river/canoe travellers interested in practical and anecdotal guidance from a colonial-era travelogue
extracted.subtask_description: Practical, narrative guidance and experiential rules-of-thumb for travelling and handling a native canoe on the Ogowe: navigating rapids, using local help and equipment, seasonal planning, and cave/river-safety cautions drawn from first‑person travel observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandbank handling and escaping
rubrics_metrics.description: When sandbanks show, they rise above the water in a slope, the low end or tail against the current; the downstream end terminates in an abrupt miniature cliff, sometimes six and seven feet above the water; you will stick on them in a canoe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "Your best way of getting off is to push on in the direction of the current, carefully preparing for the shock of suddenly coming off the cliff end." Example: the author repeatedly stuck on sandbanks and found pushing with the current best; anticipate the abrupt drop and prepare for shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for ascending rapids (use bank shelter and dodge rocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: When ascending rapids, keep as closely as possible to the most advisable bank and dodge behind every rock to profit by the shelter it affords from the current.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation and example: coming up you can cling to sheltering spits and reefs and make use of slower water near banks; the author's crew did this repeatedly to make progress against a powerful current. Prepare poles and manpower for pushing and hauling when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for descending rapids (seek the central current and keep head straight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coming down big rapids is more dangerous than coming up; fallen-tree-fringed banks and rocks become hazards when descending, so keep in the very centre of the swiftest part of the current to avoid them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "All you have got to do is to keep your canoe-head straight—quite straight, you understand—for any failure so to do will land you the other side of the tomb." Practical warning: hold a straight heading through long downhill stretches and be aware of elbow turns and reefs that can make lower rapids especially severe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare and equip with poles, paddles and a stocked supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting rapids, carefully provide yourselves with a new stock of poles (and paddles) to use when fighting rapids and climbing over ridges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the voyage: the travellers stocked up on poles and used hands, poles, and paddles to cling to banks and lift the canoe over a ridge. Having spare equipment is repeatedly presented as essential for managing shallows and rocky ridges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experienced local guides/crew
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsidise or take along a native to come with you and help fight the rapids; local men (e.g., Adoomas, Kembe islanders) have knowledge of channels, rapids, and life-saving local practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes relying on his Kembe island man for channel knowledge and traditions (e.g., identification of whirlpools, cave-related hazards, and rescue shrubs). Local crew also sing and help with practical navigation; paying/using native assistance is pragmatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonal planning: account for wet vs dry season changes
rubrics_metrics.description: River behaviour and navigability change dramatically with the season; the wet season can submerge sandbanks, raise river levels by many feet, and make previously passable routes impassable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that places negotiable in the dry season could be impossible in the wet season (e.g., caves flooded, ridges submerged), and that some rapids would be far worse. Plan crew size and timing accordingly—small crews that manage in dry season may not be able to ascend in wet season.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cave exploration safety and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Cave mouths along the river may be passable at current water levels but can be long, narrow, rise and fall, require crawling, and contain bats, hedgehogs, and snakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice and examples: do not enter caves without appropriate "bush lights"; the author declines to explore further for lack of lights and admits fear of caves. One Frenchman explored and found wildlife. Sub-fluvial caves can create whirlpools—exercise caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and use natural lifesaving aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain shrubs and plants (e.g., a long-branched willow-like shrub on Kondo Kondo) are regarded by natives as life lines because their tough branches can be used by a man thrown into the water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local knowledge: the Adooma emphasized this shrub as the only thing that helped a man when his canoe got thrown over in the Alemba. Learn local rescue resources and use them when available; check for wedged items indicating past accidents (e.g., a knife and belt wedged among rocks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to being stuck/overturned among rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: If you get on to partially submerged table rocks or are upset among rocks, push and shove the canoe free and re-embark when possible; when wrung across the river, use poles and cooperative effort to regain control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the crew were up to their knees in water pushing the canoe free after being swept across; the author describes several near-misses with pinnacle rocks and being 'bundled off' table rocks by the river that then unceremoniously released them back into the flow. Practical emphasis on teamwork, immediate physical effort, and avoidance of needle-like pinnacles.
